lesson_title: Eight Blocks Across, Six Blocks Up: Distance, Midpoint and Gradient
hook_text: Fourteen blocks by the streets. Ten blocks across the grass. That gap IS the distance formula.
clip_script: A suburb on a grid. You're at the school gate; the library is eight blocks east and six blocks north. Follow the streets and that's fourteen blocks. But the sports fields are wide open — cut straight across. How far? Eight across, six up: a right-angled triangle. Sixty-four plus thirty-six is one hundred. Square root — ten. Ten blocks, four saved. That is the whole distance formula; coordinates just hand you the eight and the six without counting. Now the middle. Friends at house five and house seventeen meet at house eleven — add and halve. On a grid you do it twice: once across, once up. Brand this in: middle means ADD and halve. Distance and steepness both SUBTRACT. And steepness? Gradient is up divided by across — rise over run. Four over three means every three steps forward, four steps up — steeper than forty-five degrees. Flat court: zero. Straight wall: undefined, not zero — there's no across to divide by. Right angles? Flip one gradient, switch its sign, multiply — get negative one and the angle is proved. No protractor, just arithmetic.
visual_style: Overhead grid-suburb animation: street route in one colour, diagonal shortcut in another; house numbers averaging to a meeting point; a mall ramp against a mountain pass tilting to show gradient; two lines snapping perpendicular with −1 flashing.
pacing: Quick through the walk, a beat on 'ten', deliberate on the add-versus-subtract rule.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and classify any quadrilateral on the grid without guessing.
